ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Vascular Neurology Referral — Liliʻuokalani

code.originalText: Urgent visit the morning after 20 minutes of right hand weakness and word-finding difficulty: examination, ABCD2 score, ECG and same-day emergency stroke evaluation with CT, CT angiography, swallow screen and antiplatelet loading, with culturally safe care and her ʻohana present at her choice

text.paragraph: About 20 minutes of right hand weakness and word-finding difficulty yesterday afternoon in a 78-year-old woman, fully resolved, ABCD2 score 5. Same-day emergency evaluation today; please see her at the rapid-access stroke clinic tomorrow morning to confirm the diagnosis, find the cause and set her secondary prevention plan. [S]
Urgency: Urgent; emergency department stroke evaluation today and the rapid-access stroke clinic tomorrow morning. [S]

list.item: Is this a transient ischemic attack or a minor ischemic stroke, and what is its most likely cause?
Do you agree with 21 days of aspirin and clopidogrel, and what should follow it?
What rhythm monitoring do you advise, and what should we do if atrial fibrillation is found?
Does the carotid plaque need treatment or follow-up imaging?
What blood pressure and LDL targets, and which screening for swallowing, cognition, mood and falls, do you advise?

text.paragraph: Native Hawaiian elder and composer, who asked to be called Liliʻuokalani; she leads her own decisions and wants members of her ʻohana present. Yesterday afternoon, while playing the piano, her right hand became weak and clumsy and she could not find her words for about 20 minutes; both recovered fully. Told of borderline blood pressure in past years, never treated. No diabetes, no prior stroke, never smoked, alcohol rarely. Today: blood pressure 156/88 mmHg, pulse 72 and regular; NIH Stroke Scale 0; ECG sinus rhythm without atrial fibrillation. ABCD2 score 5 (age 1, blood pressure 1, unilateral weakness 2, duration 10 to 59 minutes 1). Sent to the emergency department for CT, CT angiography of the head and neck, a swallow screen and laboratory tests, with aspirin and clopidogrel loading if no hemorrhage is seen. Atorvastatin 40 mg started. Native Hawaiian healing offered alongside clinic care at her choice [S]

list.item: She wants to keep playing and composing, and fears losing the use of her right hand or her words. [S]
She wants her ʻohana involved as she chooses, and her own Native Hawaiian ways of healing respected. [S]
She wants to be told plainly what is planned and to make her own decisions. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Liliʻuokalani was born on September 2, 1838, in Honolulu, at her family's home at Pūowaina, to Analeʻa Keohokālole and Caesar Kapaʻakea; in her memoir she wrote that she was born near the site of the later Queen's Hospital, on Sept. 2, 1838. [D]

Her birth name was Lydia Liliʻu Loloku Walania Wewehi Kamakaʻeha. She became the hānai (adopted) daughter of High Chief Abner Pākī and Chiefess Laura Kōnia, and was baptized as a Christian with the name Lydia Kamakaʻeha Pākī. [D]
From 1842 she was educated at the Chiefs' Children's School, founded by Kamehameha III for young royals. [D]
In 1862 she married John Owen Dominis and moved to Washington Place in Honolulu, where she lived for 55 years, until her death; her husband died in 1891. [D]

She was a musician and composer of more than 150 songs, including "Aloha ʻOe" (1878) and He Mele Lāhui Hawaiʻi, the kingdom's national anthem from 1866; she played the piano and ukulele and wrote musical notation. [D]
She became queen in 1891, on the death of her brother King Kalākaua, the last reigning monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom. [D]

On January 16, 1893, the United States Minister and naval representatives caused armed naval forces of the United States to invade the sovereign Hawaiian nation and position themselves near ʻIolani Palace to intimidate the Queen and her government; on January 17 the kingdom was overthrown, and to avoid bloodshed she yielded her authority, under protest, to the United States rather than to the Provisional Government. [D]

After a failed attempt to restore her to the throne in 1895, she was arrested and imprisoned in ʻIolani Palace, where on January 24, 1895, she was forced by representatives of the Republic of Hawaii to abdicate; she was held in the palace for about eight months, translating the Kumulipo and composing songs, and was later released and pardoned. Her memoir captions a picture of the palace: "My palace was my prison." [D]
A lifelong Christian and member of Kawaiahaʻo Church, she was baptized into the Episcopal faith in 1896. [D]

The United States annexed Hawaiʻi in 1898, the year she published her memoir, Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen; in 1909 she executed a Deed of Trust for the benefit of orphan and other destitute children in the Hawaiian Islands. [D]

list.item: Native Hawaiian elder (kupuna), composer, musician and leader of her people; lives at Washington Place, her home of many years, in Honolulu, with members of her household; asked to be called Liliʻuokalani [S]
Speaks Hawaiian and English; chose English for her visits, with Hawaiian words where she prefers them; reads and writes music daily and plays the piano [S]
ʻOhana: she wants members of her ʻohana, including those joined to her by hānai, present when decisions are made, and she makes the decisions; she does not want to be a burden to them [S]
Faith: a lifelong Christian and member of her church; she prays daily; the hospital chaplain was offered and she will ask for her own minister if she wishes [S]

History: she lived through the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, backed by U.S. forces, imprisonment in her own palace and a forced abdication; she spoke of it briefly and with composure, and said she wants to be told plainly what is planned and to decide for herself [S]

Traditional healing: she has her own Native Hawaiian practices and practitioners and will decide whether and how they are part of her care; lomilomi through a Native Hawaiian Health Care System and hoʻoponopono with her ʻohana were offered alongside clinic care, and nothing further was asked [S]
Diet: fish, poi and kalo, greens, fruit and rice, with some salted fish and preserved foods; never smoked; alcohol rarely, a glass of wine on occasions [S]
Strengths, supports and purpose: her music, her faith, her ʻohana, her work for the welfare of Hawaiian children, and a steadfast, composed manner [S]

list.item: Transient weakness and clumsiness of the right hand with word-finding difficulty, lasting about 20 minutes and fully resolved, the afternoon before the visit; suspected transient ischemic attack, ABCD2 score 5 (high risk); NIH Stroke Scale 0: active, provisional [S]
Hypertension: told of borderline readings in past years and not treated; 156/88 mmHg at intake: active, confirmed [S]

Culturally safe, trauma-informed care: address her as Liliʻuokalani, as she asked; take time; explain each test and treatment plainly before it is done; involve her ʻohana as she chooses while she makes the decisions; acknowledge the history of the overthrow when she raises it, without probing. Guideline: Primary Care of Adult Patients After Stroke: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); Ke Ola Mamo: a Native Hawaiian Health Care System serving Oʻahu (medical care, lomilomi and community health workers) (2026); Public Law 103-150: joint resolution to acknowledge the 100th anniversary of the January 17, 1893 overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii, and to offer an apology to Native Hawaiians (1993) [S]

Dual antiplatelet therapy started within 24 hours of onset once CT excluded bleeding: aspirin 325 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg loading doses, then aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 21 days, then a single antiplatelet; stop antiplatelets if anticoagulation is started. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); Clopidogrel and Aspirin in Acute Ischemic Stroke and High-Risk TIA (POINT) (2018); Clopidogrel with aspirin in acute minor stroke or transient ischemic attack (CHANCE) (2013) [S]

Atorvastatin 40 mg daily, a high-intensity statin, with a lipid panel at four to twelve weeks; LDL goal below 70 mg/dL. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke and transient ischemic attack, atrial fibrillation and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Bedside swallow screen before any food or drink, a cognition screen (MoCA) at the stroke clinic, a depression screen, and a falls assessment. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); Primary Care of Adult Patients After Stroke: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke and transient ischemic attack, atrial fibrillation and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

BE FAST: balance, eyes, face, arm, speech, time to call 911; call 911 at once for any new symptom, even if it passes, and do not drive herself. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); Signs and Symptoms of Stroke (2026) [S]

Native Hawaiian healing alongside clinic care, if she wishes: lomilomi through Ke Ola Mamo, a Native Hawaiian Health Care System, with the practitioner told that she takes blood thinners, and hoʻoponopono with her ʻohana as they choose; the clinic asks nothing further about her practices. Guideline: Ke Ola Mamo: a Native Hawaiian Health Care System serving Oʻahu (medical care, lomilomi and community health workers) (2026) [S]

Daily walking, the foods she already eats with less salted and preserved food, alcohol kept to rare occasions, and no smoking. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke and transient ischemic attack, atrial fibrillation and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]
Referral to vascular neurology, Henrik Abernethy-Sato, MD, ordered 2026-03-16 [S]
